rules.specification: Interpret clarity as allowing a user to identify the page's subject or purpose from its title, including when the title is encountered separately in search results.
rules.violation_condition: A page title is too vague, misleading or unclear to identify the page's subject or purpose.
rules.why: G-1: title clarity is a distinct textual requirement within the accessibility section.

rules.quote: Organise content in a clear order using section headings.
rules.specification: This check concerns using headings to expose the content's sections. Assess the ordering of existing headings under the more specific heading-hierarchy rule.
rules.violation_condition: Content with distinct sections lacks section headings that mark and organise those sections.
when: Applies where the content has distinct sections to organise.
rules.why: G-1: section-heading presence is distinct from heading wording and the logical ordering of existing headings.

rules.quote: Describe the topics or the following section in the headings.
rules.violation_condition: A heading does not describe the topic or content of the section it introduces.
rules.why: G-1: descriptive heading wording is independently checkable and is not the same requirement as providing or ordering headings.

covers.quote: Use the type of structure that suits the content and how people will need to consume it.
Use a structure that matches expectations for the type of content you're creating:
To group content into topics or connected ideas, prioritised by level of importance, use a hierarchical structure.
To present a sequence of steps or events, use a sequential structure.
To guide people from beginning to end, use a narrative structure.

rules.quote: Pick the type of structure that works for the user
rules.specification: The page supplies three purpose-based cases but no objective test for user expectations, unconventional structure or inconsistency. Those judgments need the content's purpose and audience context.
rules.violation_condition: The content uses an organising structure that does not suit its purpose or users' expectations, or applies its structure unconventionally or inconsistently in a way that impedes finding and understanding information.
when: Use a hierarchical structure to group topics or connected ideas, prioritised by importance.
Use a sequential structure to present a sequence of steps or events.
Use a narrative structure to guide readers through an entire story from beginning to end.
The structure should be conventional and consistent for its purpose and users.
rules.why: G-2: the three content purposes are cases of the same structure-suitability check; G-4: consolidate its summaries and warning against unsuitable structural conventions.

rules.quote: Use a logical hierarchy or sequential steps for headings.
rules.violation_condition: Existing headings are arranged in an illogical hierarchy or an illogical sequence of steps.
when: Headings may follow either a logical hierarchy or a sequence of steps, as appropriate to the content.
rules.why: G-2: hierarchy and sequential steps are alternative cases of one heading-organisation check.

rules.quote: Write a topic sentence for each paragraph.
rules.violation_condition: A paragraph has no topic sentence expressing its main idea.
rules.why: G-1: topic-sentence presence is a specific check beneath the scan-friendly design section.

rules.quote: Display important information in lists, callout boxes, tables and illustrations.
rules.specification: The listed formats are ways to display information, not a requirement to use all four. The page does not define which information is important enough to require this treatment.
rules.violation_condition: Important information remains only in undifferentiated running text rather than being displayed in a suitable list, callout box, table or illustration.
when: Applies to information important enough to warrant prominent or structured display.
rules.why: G-2: the display formats are alternative implementations of one information-presentation requirement.

rules.quote: Structure your content by writing about one idea at a time:
rules.specification: Supporting details that develop the same main idea do not count as competing ideas. Flag competing lines of discussion, not merely several facts supporting one point.
rules.violation_condition: A passage interleaves distinct ideas rather than developing one idea at a time.
rules.why: G-1: the lead-in states an idea-focus requirement distinct from the list's ordering, grouping and paragraph-length checks.

rules.quote: Start with the most important idea first.
rules.specification: Determining the most important idea requires the content's purpose and users' needs; the page gives no independent ranking criterion.
rules.violation_condition: The content starts with a less important idea while its most important idea is introduced later.
rules.why: G-1: priority at the start of the content is a distinct ordering check.

rules.violation_condition: Related ideas are scattered across heading sections, or a heading section combines unrelated groups of ideas.
rules.why: G-1: grouping content by relationship is distinct from the wording and hierarchy of its headings.

rules.specification: The page gives no word-count or sentence-count threshold for a short paragraph. A reviewer must establish a threshold before a length-based checker can make findings.
rules.violation_condition: Ideas are presented in paragraphs that are not short.
rules.why: G-1: paragraph length is independently checkable; E-4: do not invent a numerical threshold.

rules.quote: Make sure ideas flow from one paragraph to the next.
rules.specification: Assess whether the connection between adjacent paragraphs is understandable. An explicit transition word is not required when the connection is already clear.
rules.violation_condition: Adjacent paragraphs make an abrupt or unexplained shift that leaves the relationship between their ideas unclear.
rules.why: G-1: coherence between paragraphs is distinct from paragraph length and sentence order.

rules.quote: Use a logical order for sentences.
rules.violation_condition: Sentences are sequenced so that the progression of ideas, events or instructions is illogical or difficult to follow.
rules.why: G-1: sentence sequencing is a separate check from transitions between paragraphs.
